title: Free a native buffer once, whether or not it was closed

blocks.text: An image service decodes into buffers outside the Java heap. `NativeBuffer` takes its memory from an `Allocator` and must give the address back with `free`. Most code closes its buffers with try-with-resources, but a few code paths forget, and the service's native memory climbs until the container is killed. Freeing an address twice is worse: it corrupts the allocator.

items: `register(cleaner)`: what frees the buffer's memory if nobody closes it;

blocks.text: When you're done, every buffer's address is freed exactly once: at `close()` if it is closed, and otherwise after a garbage collection finds the buffer unreachable. About four lines in total.
The tests give each buffer its own `Cleaner`, ask the JVM for collections with `System.gc()`, and wait up to ten seconds for a forgotten buffer to be freed.

cases.says: closing a buffer, for example at the end of try-with-resources, frees its address at once
a second close() frees nothing more
a buffer nobody closed is freed after a collection finds it unreachable
a buffer that was closed is not freed a second time when it is later collected

origin.section: A Cleaner Runs After a Collection Finds Its Object, So close() Is the Release You Can Count On

concepts: A cleaning action that refers to its object, such as a lambda reading a field, keeps the object reachable from the Cleaner, so it is never cleaned.
A Cleaner's action runs only after a collection finds its object unreachable, never if no collection happens; close() through the Cleanable releases at once and only once.
